glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 28 sets the bold righteous against the fleeing wicked in how they treat God’s law, use power over the poor, and pursue riches, and at its center it promises mercy to the sinner who stops covering his sins.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 28 begins the last part of the proverbs of Solomon copied by Hezekiah’s men (25:1–29:27). The word pictures of chapters 25–27 give way here to direct contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, with rulers and the poor often in view.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Proverbs 28:1–11 — Keeping the Law and Walking in Integrity

  • Proverbs 28:12–18 — Confession, Reverence, and Rulers

  • Proverbs 28:19–28 — Hastening to Be Rich and Trusting the LORD

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “He who covers his sins will not prosper, But whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy.” (Proverbs 28:13)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 28 opens with two very different men: “The wicked flee when no one pursues, But the righteous are bold as a lion” (28:1). Guilt makes a person afraid of shadows, while a clear conscience before God gives courage. The sayings that follow tie that difference to God’s law. Those who forsake it praise the wicked, “But those who seek the LORD understand all” (28:5), and the man who will not hear the law finds that “Even his prayer is an abomination” (28:9).

At the center stands the plainest word of mercy in Proverbs: “He who covers his sins will not prosper, But whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (28:13). Verse 14 adds a lasting reverence, the fear of the LORD that keeps a heart from hardening. The God who refuses the prayer of a man who will not hear His law meets the confessing sinner with mercy.

Around that center, a wicked ruler over poor people is “a roaring lion and a charging bear” (28:15), and the man who hastens after riches does not consider that poverty is coming (28:22). Hiding runs through the chapter: people hide when the wicked rise (28:12, 28), eyes are hidden from the poor (28:27), and the sinner covers his sins (28:13). Mercy comes only when what is covered is confessed.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 28:1–11 — Keeping the Law and Walking in Integrity

The section begins with the fear that guilt produces and the courage of a clear conscience, then shows how a person’s response to God’s law comes out in whom he admires, what he understands, the company he keeps, and even his prayers. Among these sayings, a poor man’s integrity outweighs crooked wealth, a poor man who oppresses the poor is like rain that flattens the crops, usury’s gains pass to one who pities the poor, and the man who leads the upright astray falls into his own pit.

Proverbs 28:12–18 — Confession, Reverence, and Rulers

After a saying about how a whole community celebrates or hides depending on who rises to power, the section promises mercy to the one who confesses and forsakes his sins and calls the always-reverent man happy while warning that a hardened heart falls into calamity. It then turns to rulers who are wicked or lack understanding and so prey on the poor, to the bloodguilty man whom no one should shield, and to the safety of the one who walks blamelessly.

Proverbs 28:19–28 — Hastening to Be Rich and Trusting the LORD

Steady work and faithfulness are set against frivolous pursuits, a judgment that can be bought for bread, and the grasping eye that rushes after riches without considering that poverty is coming. The closing sayings value honest rebuke above flattery, expose the son who robs his parents and says, “It is no transgression” (28:24), set pride and self-trust against trust in the LORD, and commend giving to the poor, before the last verse echoes verse 12 and adds that when the wicked perish, the righteous increase.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 28 answers a question the book’s earlier warnings raise: what hope is there for someone already on the wrong path? For anyone who has followed the young man of chapter 7 into sin, the way back is confession that forsakes the sin, met by mercy (28:13). David knew it: “my iniquity I have not hidden,” “And You forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5). In Christ the promise is complete: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). This mercy is God’s gift, received in confession, never earned by it.

The chapter also speaks to anyone who holds authority, from a king to a parent or employer. Power that serves greed preys on the weak, while a ruler who “hates covetousness will prolong his days” (28:16).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Guilt and boldness. A guilty conscience runs from shadows and drives the bloodguilty man toward the pit, while the righteous stand without fear (28:1, 17).

Hearing God’s law. Keeping the law shows in whom a person praises or resists, what he understands, the company he keeps, and whether his prayer is acceptable (28:4–5, 7, 9).

Covering and confessing. Hidden sin does not prosper, but confession joined to forsaking receives mercy, and constant reverence keeps the heart soft (28:13–14).

Rulers and the people under them. A rebellious land churns through rulers, and wicked rule sends people into hiding and turns power against the poor, while understanding and a hatred of covetousness bring stability (28:2, 12, 15–16, 28).

Integrity, haste, and generosity. Integrity outweighs riches, haste for wealth ends in want, and the one who gives to the poor will not lack, a description of God’s ways rather than a formula for financial return (28:6, 8, 20, 22, 27).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The law (28:4, 7, 9). The Hebrew word is torah. In this collection it means God’s instruction, and keeping it marks a son as discerning. Refusing to hear it turns even prayer into an abomination, though God never turns away the cry of the repentant (compare 15:8).

Always reverent (28:14). A steady fear of the LORD, a right view of God that brings awe at His holiness and keeps a person tender toward Him. Its opposite is the heart that hardens and falls into calamity.

Usury and extortion (28:8). Charging interest to the needy and taking what belongs to others by pressure or fraud. The saying insists that wealth gathered this way will pass to someone who pities the poor.

An evil eye (28:22). A grasping, greedy outlook that hurries after riches. The book’s portrait of the greedy, the one who “hastens to be rich” (28:20), is completed here by a man so focused on gain that he does not consider the poverty coming toward him.

Trusts in his own heart (28:26). Relying on one’s own inner impulses as a guide. Proverbs calls the heart something to be kept “with all diligence” (4:23) and tells the reader to “lean not on your own understanding” (3:5); here the self-trusting man is called a fool, while “whoever walks wisely,” with skill for living God’s way, “will be delivered.”

outline: Proverbs 28:1–11 — Keeping the Law and Walking in Integrity
Proverbs 28:19–28 — Hastening to Be Rich and Trusting the LORD

sections.title: Keeping the Law and Walking in Integrity
Hastening to Be Rich and Trusting the LORD

1.brief: A guilty conscience makes the wicked run when no one is chasing them, while the righteous stand as bold as a lion. Their boldness is the confidence of a clear conscience before God, and this opening contrast between fear and courage sets the tone for the righteous-and-wicked sayings of chapters 28–29.
1.explain:
“The wicked flee when no one pursues,” The wicked man runs, though no one is chasing him. His guilt makes him afraid. He hears footsteps that are not there and sees threats in shadows. A guilty conscience does not need an actual enemy to fill a person with fear; it supplies its own. The Law warned that the disobedient would “flee when no one pursues” (Leviticus 26:17).

“But the righteous are bold as a lion.” The righteous man stands his ground. Like the lion of 30:30, which does not turn away from any beast, he faces what comes without panic. His boldness is not aggression or arrogance; it is the confidence of a clear conscience before God. He has nothing to hide, so he has nothing to fear from exposure.

This opening saying sets the tone for chapters 28–29, which return to direct contrasts between the righteous and the wicked after the many comparisons of chapters 25–27. It locates the difference first in the inner life: guilt produces fear, and righteousness before God produces courage. The chapter will later show where the guilty can find relief, in confession and mercy (28:13).
1.notes: Chapters 28–29 contain many sayings in which the two lines contrast the righteous and the wicked, much like 10:1–15:33. Several of them concern rulers and the effect of righteous or wicked leadership on a whole community (28:2, 12, 15–16, 28).

2.brief: When a land is full of rebellion, its rulers come and go in quick succession, but a man of understanding and knowledge brings lasting order. A nation’s sin breeds instability, while wise leadership allows what is right to endure.
2.explain:
“Because of the transgression of a land, many are its princes;” When a nation is full of rebellion against God and His ways, its rulers change rapidly. One leader falls and another rises, through plots, revolts or assassinations. Instability at the top reflects corruption throughout the land. Sin does not stay private; it weakens the whole nation and makes stable government hard to keep.

“But by a man of understanding and knowledge Right will be prolonged.” In contrast, a single wise and knowledgeable leader can bring lasting order. Understanding and knowledge here are moral and practical wisdom, the ability to see what is right and govern accordingly. Under such a man, what is right is prolonged: justice and stability endure.

The saying ties a nation’s stability to its moral condition and to the character of its leaders. It applies to every level of authority, from nations to communities and households, and it describes the general way God has ordered His world rather than predicting the fate of a particular government.
2.notes:
Israel’s northern kingdom illustrates the first line: it saw many changes of dynasty, several by assassination, in its last decades (2 Kings 15). The proverb itself names no nation.

The second line is compressed in Hebrew, and translations render it in different ways. The word the NKJV translates “Right” can mean right or just, and a Hebrew word spelled the same way is the ordinary word for “so,” which is how the NASB reads it. The NKJV’s “Right will be prolonged” and the NASB’s reading both express lasting stability under a wise ruler.

3.brief: Oppression by a poor man against others who are poor is like a beating rain that flattens the crops instead of watering them. Rain ought to bring food, yet this storm leaves none, and the one who knows poverty from the inside should be the last to exploit it.
3.explain:
“A poor man who oppresses the poor” Here is a man who knows poverty from the inside, yet he takes advantage of others who are poor. Perhaps he has gained a little power or position, and he uses it to squeeze those beneath him. He should understand their struggles better than anyone, which makes his oppression especially bitter.

“Is like a driving rain which leaves no food.” Rain normally brings food, watering the crops and producing a harvest. But a driving, beating rain flattens the grain and washes away the soil, leaving nothing. The man who should have been a help has become a destroyer.

The saying warns that oppression is not limited to the rich and powerful. Anyone with a little power over others can misuse it, and the poor can be cruel to the poor. Knowing hardship should make a person compassionate. When it does not, the result is like a storm that ruins the very fields it should have watered.
3.notes: In Hebrew the man in the first line is described with a word meaning “poor,” and the NKJV, ESV, NASB, KJV and NLT translate it that way. The 1984 NIV reads “A ruler” instead.

4.brief: People who abandon God’s law end up praising the wicked, but those who keep it stand up and oppose them. How a person treats God’s instruction shows in whom he admires and whom he resists.
4.explain:
“Those who forsake the law praise the wicked,” The law here is God’s instruction, the teaching He has given His people. Those who abandon it lose their moral bearings. They begin to admire and praise wicked people, approving their success, excusing their conduct, even celebrating them. Turning from God’s instruction changes what a person values.

“But such as keep the law contend with them.” Those who keep God’s law oppose the wicked. They resist them, speak against their ways, and refuse to approve what God condemns. Their loyalty to God’s instruction shows in their stance toward evil.

The saying shows that a person’s response to God’s law reveals itself in whom he admires and whom he resists. Neutrality is not really possible. Keeping God’s instruction produces discernment and courage, while forsaking it leads to confusion about right and wrong. The contending here is not quarrelsomeness; it is faithful resistance to what is evil, the courage of 28:1 put into practice.
4.notes: The Hebrew word behind “law” is torah, which basically means instruction or teaching. It appears four times in three nearby verses, twice in 28:4 and once each in 28:7 and 28:9. In Proverbs the word can mean a parent’s teaching (1:8) as well as God’s instruction; in these sayings it stands for God’s instruction to His people.

5.brief: Evil men cannot grasp what justice really is, “But those who seek the LORD understand all.” Moral understanding comes from seeking the LORD Himself, and those who turn from Him lose the ability to see right and wrong clearly.
5.explain:
“Evil men do not understand justice,” Evil men cannot grasp what justice really is. Their own wickedness clouds their moral vision. They may speak of fairness, but they do not truly understand right and wrong because they do not want to. Persistent sin dulls the ability to see clearly.

“But those who seek the LORD understand all.” Those who seek the LORD understand all that matters for living rightly. This is not a claim to unlimited knowledge, as though seekers of God knew every fact. It is moral understanding: the ability to see what is just and what is wise. Such understanding comes from seeking God Himself.

The saying connects moral discernment with relationship to God. People do not discover justice by cleverness alone; it is learned by seeking the One who is just. This fits the book’s foundation: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). A right view of God opens the way to a right view of everything else.

6.brief: A poor man who walks in integrity is better off than a rich man whose ways are crooked. Character outweighs wealth, a truth already stated in 19:1 and repeated here at the start of this collection’s contrasts.
6.explain:
“Better is the poor who walks in his integrity” Integrity means wholeness, a life that is consistent and honest. A poor man who walks in integrity has little money, but he has a clean conscience and a straight path. “Than one perverse in his ways, though he be rich.” A rich man whose ways are crooked has wealth, but his life is twisted. He gains by deceit and lives by double standards.

The saying declares that the first is better. Character outweighs wealth. The poor man of integrity has something money cannot buy, while the crooked rich man has gained the world at the cost of his soul. This repeats the thought of 19:1 nearly word for word in its first line, now set at the head of a collection rich in contrasts between the righteous and the wicked.

The verse does not praise poverty for its own sake, and it does not condemn wealth as such. It compares integrity with crookedness and declares integrity better, whatever the bank balance. A person should choose integrity even if it costs him financially.
6.notes: “Perverse in his ways” translates a Hebrew phrase in which “ways” has a special form used for things that come in twos. The wording pictures a man trying to walk two ways at once, living a double or two-faced life. The same expression returns in 28:18.

7.brief: Keeping God’s law marks a son as truly discerning, but one who runs with gluttons brings shame on his father. The company a son keeps shows whether he has taken his father’s teaching to heart.
7.explain:
“Whoever keeps the law is a discerning son,” A son who keeps God’s instruction proves himself discerning. He shows that he understands what matters and has taken his father’s teaching to heart. The law here again is God’s instruction, which a wise father passes on to his son.

“But a companion of gluttons shames his father.” A son who runs with gluttons, people given to excess, waste and self-indulgence, brings shame on his father. His companions show his values, and his choices reflect badly on the one who raised him. The book has already warned the son, “Do not mix with winebibbers, Or with gluttonous eaters” (23:20).

The saying ties together obedience to God and the company one keeps. A son’s friends reveal whether he has received his father’s teaching. Keeping God’s law and keeping wise company go hand in hand, and both bring honor to a father, as 27:11 has already said.

8.brief: Wealth piled up by charging interest to the needy and by extortion will not stay with the one who gathered it; it ends up with someone who is kind to the poor. What was taken from the poor finds its way back to their benefit under God’s just rule.
8.explain:
“One who increases his possessions by usury and extortion” Usury here means charging interest to the needy, and extortion means taking more than is right by pressure or fraud. The Law of Moses forbade Israelites to charge interest on loans to their poor brothers: “you shall not be like a moneylender to him; you shall not charge him interest” (Exodus 22:25). This man builds his wealth by exploiting those who are already struggling.

“Gathers it for him who will pity the poor.” Yet his wealth will not stay with him. In the end it passes to someone who shows kindness to the poor. What was taken from the poor finds its way back to their benefit. The man thinks he is gathering for himself, but he is gathering for someone else.

The saying affirms God’s justice working through the course of events. Proverbs has said something similar: “the wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous” (13:22). This is a description of God’s moral order, not a promise that every exploiter will lose his fortune in his lifetime or that wealth will automatically come to believers. It warns that wealth gained by oppression is not secure, and that God sees and cares for the poor.
8.notes: The Law also forbade interest on food lent to a poor brother (Leviticus 25:36–37). The two Hebrew words behind “usury and extortion” both refer to forms of interest or profit taken from a loan.

9.brief: When a man refuses to listen to God’s law, even his prayer becomes an abomination. Prayer cannot cover a life that stubbornly will not hear God; the warning concerns persistent refusal, not the cry of the repentant (compare 15:8).
9.explain:
“One who turns away his ear from hearing the law,” This man refuses to listen to God’s instruction. He turns his ear away deliberately; he does not want to hear what God says about how he should live. This is persistent refusal, a settled unwillingness to be taught or corrected by God.

“Even his prayer is an abomination.” Strikingly, even his prayer is detestable to God. Prayer is meant to be communion with God, but this man wants to speak to God while refusing to hear Him. His prayer becomes an attempt to use God without submitting to Him. Proverbs has said, “The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, But the prayer of the upright is His delight” (15:8).

The warning concerns a person who keeps on refusing to hear God, not the cry of someone who is turning back. The repentant sinner who comes to God with a broken heart is not rejected; the very next section promises mercy to the one who confesses and forsakes his sins (28:13). What God rejects is religious activity that covers a heart that will not listen. Prayer cannot stand in for obedience.

10.brief: Whoever leads upright people into an evil way will fall into his own pit, while the blameless will inherit good. Leading others astray is a trap that snaps shut on the one who sets it.
10.explain:
“Whoever causes the upright to go astray in an evil way,” This man deliberately leads good people into wrongdoing. He tempts, deceives or pressures the upright to abandon their integrity. Corrupting others is a serious evil, because it multiplies wickedness and destroys what was good. “He himself will fall into his own pit;” The trap he sets for others catches him instead. The pit he dug for the upright becomes his own grave. Proverbs has already said, “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (26:27).

“But the blameless will inherit good.” In contrast, those who remain blameless will receive good as their inheritance. The upright who resist the tempter, or whom God preserves, end up with blessing.

The verse has three lines instead of the usual two. It sets the corrupter’s self-destruction beside the blameless person’s reward, and it warns anyone tempted to lead others into sin that he is digging a pit for himself.

11.brief: Riches can leave a man wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with understanding sees right through him. Wealth breeds self-confidence, yet it cannot hide a person from the discernment of someone truly wise.
11.explain:
“The rich man is wise in his own eyes,” Wealth often brings self-confidence. The rich man assumes his success proves his wisdom. He thinks he knows best because he has done well, and he may become closed to correction. “But the poor who has understanding searches him out.” A poor man who has understanding sees through him. He examines the rich man’s claims and recognizes the pride and folly behind his confidence. His lack of wealth does not prevent him from seeing clearly.

The saying shows that wealth and wisdom are not the same. Riches can make a person feel wise without making him so. Meanwhile, understanding can belong to someone without money or status. The verse does not say every poor person is wise or every rich person foolish; it says the poor man who has understanding can see what the self-satisfied rich man cannot see about himself.

The phrase “wise in his own eyes” recalls the warnings of 26:12 and 3:7. Self-assessment based on success is dangerous, and true discernment can come from unexpected places.

12.brief: When the righteous triumph, there is great glory and celebration, but when the wicked rise to power, people go into hiding. The mood of a whole community follows who is in charge, and the second half of this saying returns at the chapter’s end in verse 28.
12.explain:
“When the righteous rejoice, there is great glory;” When the righteous triumph, when they are in positions of influence and things go well for them, there is great glory. The whole community celebrates. Justice prevails, people feel safe, and life flourishes. “But when the wicked arise, men hide themselves.” When wicked people rise to power, ordinary people go into hiding. They keep their heads down, avoid attention, and protect themselves from those who now hold power. Fear replaces celebration.

The saying shows that the character of those in charge affects everyone. Righteous leadership brings joy and openness; wicked leadership brings fear and concealment. The mood of a whole community follows who rises to power. Proverbs makes the same observation elsewhere: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice; But when a wicked man rules, the people groan” (29:2).

This verse opens the second section of the chapter, and its second line returns almost word for word in 28:28, where the chapter closes. The two verses frame the chapter’s concern with righteous and wicked rule and its effects on ordinary people.
12.notes:
The Hebrew of the second line says literally that a man is searched for. The KJV text says that a man is hidden, and its margin gives “sought for.” The picture is of people who disappear so completely that they have to be searched out.

Hiding and covering run through the chapter: people hide themselves when the wicked rise (28:12, 28), the sinner covers his sins (28:13), and the stingy man hides his eyes from the poor (28:27).

13.brief: Whoever hides his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses them and turns away from them will receive mercy. This is the book’s plainest word of mercy for the sinner: confessing and forsaking go together, and mercy is God’s gift to the one who stops hiding, a hope fulfilled in the cleansing Christ provides (1 John 1:9).
13.explain:
“He who covers his sins will not prosper,” To cover sin is to hide it: to deny it, excuse it, or bury it and hope no one finds out. The person who does this will not prosper. Hidden sin does not stay hidden, and it does not leave the sinner at peace. It festers, damages relationships, hardens the heart and keeps the person from God. David described what concealment did to him: “When I kept silent, my bones grew old Through my groaning all the day long” (Psalm 32:3).

“But whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy.” The alternative is to confess, to admit the sin honestly before God and, where appropriate, before others, and to forsake it, turning away and leaving it behind. Confession and forsaking go together. Confession without forsaking is empty words, and trying to forsake sin without confessing it leaves it hidden. The one who does both will have mercy. Mercy is God’s gift, not something earned by confessing; confession opens the door to receive what God freely gives. David found it so: “I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ And You forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

This is the plainest word of mercy in the book of Proverbs, and it answers the warnings of chapters 5–7 for anyone who has already fallen into sin. It points ahead to the cleansing God provides in Christ: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
13.notes:
The Hebrew verb translated “covers” is the same one used in 26:26 of hatred covered by deceit. There the covering is exposed before the assembly; here the alternative to covering is confession.

“Will have mercy” translates a Hebrew verb meaning to love deeply or to show tender compassion. The same verb appears twice in Psalm 103:13, “As a father pities his children, So the LORD pities those who fear Him,” which shows the kind of compassion the word describes.

14.brief: Happy is the person who lives in constant reverence before God, but the one who hardens his heart will fall into disaster. Verse 13 called for confession; now the call is for a lasting fear of the LORD that keeps the heart soft.
14.explain:
“Happy is the man who is always reverent,” Happy means truly blessed, living in the good condition God gives. The man who is always reverent lives in constant awe of God. This is the fear of the LORD, a right view of God that brings awe at His holiness and keeps a person tender toward Him and careful about sin. Being always reverent means this awe is not occasional; it is a steady part of his life.

“But he who hardens his heart will fall into calamity.” The opposite of reverence is a hardened heart, a heart that resists God, ignores His warnings and grows insensitive to sin. Such a person will fall into calamity. A hard heart leads to ruin, because it refuses the correction and mercy that would have saved it.

After 28:13 called for confession, this verse calls for a lasting reverence that keeps the heart soft. Confession deals with sin once it has been committed; constant reverence guards the heart against hardening in the first place. The two belong together: the confessing sinner receives mercy, and the reverent heart stays open to God.
14.notes: The Hebrew says literally that the man fears continually, without naming the object; the KJV has “feareth alway.” The ESV supplies “the LORD,” and the NLT reads “fear to do wrong.” The NKJV’s “always reverent” understands the fear as reverence toward God.

15.brief: A wicked ruler over poor people is as dangerous as a roaring lion or a charging bear. Power in wicked hands turns a ruler into a predator against those least able to defend themselves.
15.explain:
“Like a roaring lion and a charging bear” A roaring lion is terrifying and deadly, and a charging bear is just as dangerous. Both pictures show raw, destructive power aimed at the weak. “Is a wicked ruler over poor people.” A wicked ruler is like these beasts. Instead of protecting the poor, he preys on them. The people least able to defend themselves become his victims.

The saying exposes how power in wicked hands turns a ruler into a predator. Authority is meant to protect, especially the vulnerable, but a wicked ruler uses it to devour. The poor suffer most, because they have no resources to resist or escape.

The verse applies to every kind of authority, not only kings. Anyone with power over others, whether in a government, a business, a church or a family, can become a lion or a bear to those under him, and the saying warns against that abuse.
15.notes: In 28:1 the righteous are “bold as a lion.” Here the lion returns as a picture of a ruler’s cruelty, showing the same image used for courage and for menace.

16.brief: Without understanding, a ruler becomes a great oppressor, but one who hates covetousness will prolong his days. Greed lies at the root of oppressive rule, and a leader who refuses it tends to endure.
16.explain:
“A ruler who lacks understanding is a great oppressor,” A ruler without understanding, without wisdom and moral insight, becomes a great oppressor. Lacking the discernment to govern justly, he resorts to force and exploitation. Folly in leadership produces cruelty.

“But he who hates covetousness will prolong his days.” Covetousness is greed, the desire for unjust gain. A ruler who hates it will prolong his days. He will rule longer and more securely because he does not exploit his people. Moses told Israel to choose leaders who were “men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exodus 18:21).

The two lines together show that greed lies at the root of oppressive rule. The foolish ruler oppresses because he does not understand; the wise ruler endures because he refuses to be greedy. Long rule is described here as the general fruit of just leadership, not a guarantee that every righteous ruler will reign long.
16.notes: The NKJV’s “covetousness” is rendered “unjust gain” in the ESV and NASB, pointing to profit taken unjustly.

17.brief: A man weighed down by the guilt of bloodshed will flee toward the pit of death, and no one should try to shield him from justice. His own guilt drives him toward ruin.
17.explain:
“A man burdened with bloodshed will flee into a pit;” This man is weighed down by the guilt of having shed innocent blood. He is a murderer, and his guilt drives him. He will flee toward the pit, the grave. Whether through fear, the pursuit of justice or his own tormented conscience, he is headed for death. The guilt of 28:1, where the wicked flee when no one pursues, is here at its heaviest.

“Let no one help him.” Others should not try to shield him from justice. They should not hide him, protect him or help him escape the consequences of his crime. From Genesis 9:6 onward, God’s law treated the shedding of innocent blood with utmost seriousness, and the community was not to obstruct justice for a murderer.

The saying is stern. It recognizes that some guilt is so grave that those who help the guilty escape justice become partners in the wrong. It does not forbid compassion for the person or prayer for his repentance, and the mercy of 28:13 remains open to anyone who confesses. It forbids obstructing justice.
17.notes: The ESV and NASB render the first line as the guilty man being a “fugitive” until death. The NKJV, KJV and YLT speak of his fleeing to the pit.

18.brief: The one who walks blamelessly will be kept safe, but the man whose ways are crooked will fall suddenly. The contrast between the straight walk and the crooked one returns from verse 6, now with their outcomes.
18.explain:
“Whoever walks blamelessly will be saved,” To walk blamelessly is to live with integrity, consistently and honestly, without hidden wickedness. Such a person will be saved, kept safe from the dangers and disasters that befall the crooked. The word here describes deliverance from harm in this life; it is not a claim that integrity earns salvation.

“But he who is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall.” The crooked man, whose ways are twisted and double, will fall suddenly. His downfall comes without warning. He may seem secure for a time, but his crookedness catches up with him all at once.

The verse returns to the contrast of 28:6, the straight walk and the crooked one, now with their outcomes. Integrity brings security; crookedness brings sudden ruin. Like other proverbs, this describes the general pattern of God’s world, not a promise that the blameless never suffer or that the wicked always fall quickly.
18.notes: “Perverse in his ways” is the same Hebrew expression as in 28:6, with “ways” in the form used for pairs. The Hebrew word behind “suddenly” is literally “in one,” understood as all at once, as in the KJV and YLT.

19.brief: The farmer who works his own land will have plenty of bread, but the one who chases empty pursuits will have plenty of poverty. Both halves end in abundance, one of bread and the other of want, sharpening the contrast between honest work and worthless schemes.
19.explain:
“He who tills his land will have plenty of bread,” The farmer who works his own land, plowing, planting and tending it, will have plenty of food. Steady, honest labor on what has been entrusted to him produces provision. “But he who follows frivolity will have poverty enough!” The man who chases frivolity, empty pursuits, worthless schemes and get-rich-quick ideas, will have plenty too, but plenty of poverty. The exclamation gives the line a sting.

The two halves are built to match. Each man gets an abundance: one of bread, the other of want. Honest work on what is in front of you yields provision; chasing what is empty yields emptiness. The saying nearly repeats 12:11, which ends instead by calling the frivolous man “devoid of understanding.” Here the outcome is stated more sharply.

The verse begins the chapter’s last section, which deals with work, money and haste for riches. It establishes the baseline: faithful work on ordinary things is the path to provision, while the pursuit of empty things leads to want. As always in Proverbs, this is a general pattern, not a promise that hard workers never face hardship.
19.notes: The same Hebrew verb, to be satisfied or have one’s fill, stands behind “will have plenty of bread” and “will have poverty enough,” which gives the contrast its ironic edge.

20.brief: Faithfulness brings an abundance of blessings, but the man in a hurry to get rich will not escape punishment. The portrait of the greedy begins here, setting steady faithfulness against haste for gain.
20.explain:
“A faithful man will abound with blessings,” A faithful man is reliable, honest and steady. He keeps his word, does his work, and deals fairly. Such a man will abound with blessings, from God and from others who trust him. The blessings are not limited to money; they include a good name, trusted relationships and God’s favor.

“But he who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.” The man in a hurry to get rich, impatient, grasping, willing to cut corners, will not escape punishment. Haste for wealth leads to dishonesty, risky schemes and exploitation of others, and those things bring their own consequences, under God’s just rule.

The saying sets steady faithfulness against haste for gain. It opens the book’s portrait of the greedy man in this chapter, which continues in 28:22. Faithfulness may not bring sudden wealth, but it brings lasting blessing. Haste may promise quick riches, but it leads to trouble. This is not a promise that faithfulness always produces prosperity; God promises to meet needs and to bless faithfulness, but the blessings He gives take many forms.

21.brief: Showing favoritism is wrong, yet some people will betray justice for as little as a piece of bread. Partiality often starts small, and a cheap bribe can be enough to corrupt a person’s judgment.
21.explain:
“To show partiality is not good,” Partiality means favoring someone unfairly, especially in judgment, because of who he is, what he can give, or what he can do for you. In a court or any position of judgment, partiality perverts justice. The understatement “not good” is a way of saying it is seriously wrong.

“Because for a piece of bread a man will transgress.” The second line explains how easily partiality creeps in. A man will do wrong for a piece of bread, for something as small as a meal. Corruption often starts small. A cheap bribe, a small favor, a little advantage can be enough to bend someone’s judgment.

The saying warns that the line between justice and corruption can be crossed for very little. Those who hold any kind of responsibility for judging others must guard against even small temptations. Proverbs has warned against partiality in judgment before, saying, “It is not good to show partiality in judgment” (24:23).
21.notes: In Hebrew “show partiality” is literally to recognize faces, and the YLT renders it as to “discern faces.” The phrase describes judging a case by the person instead of the facts.

22.brief: Driven by a grasping, evil eye, a man rushes after riches without considering that poverty is coming for him. Greed blinds him to the ruin it brings, completing the warning of verse 20.
22.explain:
“A man with an evil eye hastens after riches,” An evil eye in Proverbs describes a grasping, stingy, greedy outlook. The man with an evil eye looks at the world with envy and covetousness, always wanting more and never willing to share. He hastens after riches, rushing and grasping to get wealthy quickly.

“And does not consider that poverty will come upon him.” He does not stop to think that his greed is leading him toward poverty. His haste blinds him. He is so focused on gain that he cannot see the ruin his grasping is bringing. The riches he chases will slip away, and the poverty he fears will come anyway.

The saying completes the warning of 28:20. Greed is self-defeating. The man who rushes after riches with a grasping heart ends up losing what he sought. In contrast, Proverbs blesses the person who “has a generous eye” and “gives of his bread to the poor” (22:9).
22.notes: The Hebrew expression translated “an evil eye” also lies behind the “miser” of 23:6, and its opposite is the “generous eye,” literally a good eye, of 22:9. The ESV renders it “stingy” here.

23.brief: The one who rebukes someone will find more favor in the end than the one who flatters. Honest correction may sting at first, but over time it earns a gratitude that flattery never wins.
23.explain:
“He who rebukes a man will find more favor afterward” Rebuking someone, correcting him honestly when he is wrong, is not easy. It may cause discomfort, resentment or conflict at first. Yet the one who rebukes will find more favor afterward. Over time, the person corrected often recognizes the value of the rebuke and becomes grateful.

“Than he who flatters with the tongue.” The flatterer tells people what they want to hear. He gains immediate approval, but his favor does not last. Eventually people see through flattery, or they suffer the consequences of following it, and they lose respect for the one who flattered them.

The saying sets honest correction against empty praise and says correction wins in the end. It encourages courage to speak the truth in love, trusting that the long-term fruit is worth the short-term discomfort. It also echoes 27:5–6, where open rebuke is better than hidden love and a friend’s faithful wounds are better than an enemy’s kisses.

24.brief: Robbing your own father or mother while insisting, “It is no transgression,” makes you a companion of the destroyer. Excusing theft from parents, however it is explained, puts a person in the company of those who wreck and ruin.
24.explain:
“Whoever robs his father or his mother,” This is a son who steals from his own parents. Perhaps he takes their property, uses up their resources, or seizes his inheritance early. It is a betrayal of the people who gave him life and raised him. “And says, ‘It is no transgression,’” He excuses himself. He tells himself it is not really stealing, since the property will be his eventually, or since family members share, or since his parents owe him. He denies that he has done anything wrong.

“The same is companion to a destroyer.” The saying refuses his excuse. Such a son is in the same company as those who destroy and ruin. Robbing parents, however it is rationalized, puts him alongside vandals and wreckers. The Law commanded honor for father and mother, and Proverbs has already warned, “He who mistreats his father and chases away his mother Is a son who causes shame and brings reproach” (19:26).

The saying exposes how people excuse wrongdoing within families. Stealing from parents is still stealing, and calling it something else does not change what it is. The excuse itself, like the deceiver’s “I was only joking!” of 26:19, adds to the offense.

25.brief: A proud heart stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be prospered. Pride grabs for itself and creates conflict, while trust rests in what God provides.
25.explain:
“He who is of a proud heart stirs up strife,” A proud heart is arrogant and grasping. It wants more for itself, more recognition, more control, more advantage, and it cannot rest content. Such a person stirs up strife, because his pride clashes with others and his grasping creates conflict. Proud people find it hard to yield, apologize or share, so quarrels follow them.

“But he who trusts in the LORD will be prospered.” The opposite of the proud, grasping heart is the heart that trusts in the LORD. Instead of reaching for everything itself, it rests in what God provides. Such a person will be prospered, cared for by God’s hand. He does not need to fight for his place, because he trusts the One who gives.

The saying contrasts two ways of seeking one’s good: grasping for it in pride, which brings conflict, and trusting God for it, which brings peace and provision. The prosperity promised is God’s care and blessing, not a guarantee of wealth. The one who trusts God looks to Him for what he needs instead of stirring up strife to get it.
25.notes: The Hebrew behind “of a proud heart” is literally wide of soul. The Hebrew word for soul can also mean appetite or desire, so the phrase pictures a desire that is never full. The ESV renders it “greedy,” and the NASB “arrogant”; the NKJV and KJV read “proud heart.”

26.brief: Trusting your own heart is folly, but walking in wisdom brings deliverance. The heart is to be guarded and directed by God’s wisdom instead of followed as an independent guide (compare 3:5).
26.explain:
“He who trusts in his own heart is a fool,” To trust in one’s own heart is to rely on one’s own impulses, feelings and judgment as the final guide. It means following one’s heart without testing it against God’s wisdom. Proverbs calls such a person a fool, because the heart is not a reliable guide on its own. It can be deceived, swayed by desire and blinded by pride.

“But whoever walks wisely will be delivered.” The alternative is to walk wisely, to live by the wisdom God gives instead of by one’s own unchecked impulses. Such a person will be delivered, rescued from the dangers that trap those who follow their own hearts.

The saying stands close to 28:25. There the contrast was pride against trust in the LORD; here it is trust in one’s own heart against walking wisely. Proverbs does not dismiss the heart. It commands, “Keep your heart with all diligence” (4:23), and “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, And lean not on your own understanding” (3:5). The heart is to be guarded and guided by God’s wisdom, not trusted as an independent authority.

27.brief: The one who gives to the poor will not lack, but the one who shuts his eyes to their need will gather many curses. God commends and cares for the generous, though this is wisdom about His ways rather than a promise that giving prevents every need or buys a return; deliberate blindness to the poor brings the curses of those who were ignored.
27.explain:
“He who gives to the poor will not lack,” The one who shares with the poor, giving generously to those in need, will not lack. God sees and cares for the generous. Proverbs has said, “He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD, And He will pay back what he has given” (19:17). Generosity reflects God’s own heart, and He looks after those who share it.

“But he who hides his eyes will have many curses.” The one who hides his eyes from the poor, who deliberately looks away and refuses to see their need, will have many curses. The curses may come from those he ignored, whose cries rise against him, and from the consequences God allows to fall on a closed heart. Deliberate blindness to need is itself a sin.

The saying is wisdom about God’s ways, not a financial formula. It does not promise that giving guarantees a return or that the generous will never face hardship. It affirms that God cares for those who care for the poor, and that refusing to see the needy is no neutral choice. The generous person can give freely, trusting God to meet his own needs.

28.brief: When the wicked rise to power, people hide; when the wicked perish, the righteous increase. The chapter ends by repeating the warning of verse 12 and then looking past it to the day the wicked fall.
28.explain:
“When the wicked arise, men hide themselves;” The chapter returns to the warning of 28:12. When wicked people rise to power, ordinary people go into hiding. They fear for their safety and stay out of sight. Wicked rule produces fear and concealment throughout a community.

“But when they perish, the righteous increase.” Yet wicked rule does not last forever. When the wicked perish, the righteous increase. They grow in number, influence and freedom. What was suppressed comes back into the open, and the community flourishes again. Proverbs has said, “when the wicked perish, there is jubilation” (11:10).

The chapter ends by looking past the present darkness to the day the wicked fall. God rules over the rise and fall of the powerful, and He does not leave His people hidden forever. This does not promise that every wicked ruler falls quickly, but it gives hope that wickedness has an end.
28.notes: The first line repeats the second line of 28:12 almost exactly, so that the chapter is framed by sayings about the rise of the wicked and the hiding of ordinary people. The next chapter continues the theme in 29:2 and 29:16.
